title: Leadership Admired Leadership People Anticipate a Negative Response in New Conversations
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Social psychologist Nicholas Epley's research program -- 120+ experiments, 30,000+ participants -- consistently finds that people dramatically underestimate how willing others are to engage with them, leading to chronic avoidance of social connections that would make their lives more satisfying. The presumption driving avoidance is that others will be uninterested, awkward, or form a negative impression -- and Epley's data shows this is almost always wrong. Three actionable findings emerge: start more conversations with strangers; ask deeper questions (people are more interesting than assumed); and trust that the interaction will improve both parties' days more than predicted. The core message: the cost of initiating connection is lower, and the payoff is higher, than intuition suggests.
points: * People's social forecasting is systematically too pessimistic: the presumption that others will be uninterested or judge us negatively leads to chronic avoidance of connections that would increase happiness, trust, and belonging. * Epley's 120+ experiments with 30,000+ participants consistently show that most conversations go better than expected, both parties feel more connected afterward, and people find small talk personally reaffirming. * Leaders who avoid initiating deeper questions because they assume the topic will feel intrusive are mistaken: people are more interesting than we assume and want to go deeper if asked. * Don't trust your social discomfort forecast: people are poor predictors of how interactions will feel, and recognizing that expectations are probably too pessimistic is the first step toward overriding them. * The cost-benefit calculation on social initiation is reliably miscalibrated: the cost of saying hello is lower, and the payoff is higher, than intuition suggests.
quotes: People are social creatures who are made happier and healthier by human connection. Yet, every day, people bypass scores of opportunities to connect.
Research suggests they incorrectly predict that interacting with those they don't know well will be awkward, uncomfortable, or unwelcome.
Most people are much more receptive than people expect. People actually enjoy new conversations, even with strangers. They find small talk and simple pleasantries personally reaffirming.

Social psychologist Nicholas Epley has conducted more than 120 experiments on social connection, involving over 30,000 participants. His overall conclusion is that people underestimate the willingness of others to engage.
Don't trust your forecasts about social discomfort. People are poor predictors of how these interactions will feel. Recognize that your expectations are probably too pessimistic.
Ask deeper questions to create more connection than expected. Many people stay at the level of weather, work, and news because they presume deeper topics will feel intrusive.
The cost of saying hello is lower, and the payoff is higher, than you think.
